name: Butter
tagline: A paid SaaS at hellobutter.io; the exact shape of the product is not something we can confirm yet.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The name is doing a lot of work here: at least four unrelated companies have shipped software called Butter, so we are not going to pretend we know which one this is. There is a live pricing page, which is decent evidence that real people pay real money for it, so it stays on the list. What we can say generically: tools in the small-team-SaaS price band usually sell one repeated workflow plus the integrations and hosting around it, and the workflow is almost always the cheap part to rebuild. The verdict is kinda on structural grounds, not on inspection, and it should be read as provisional until someone reads the product page properly. The build prompt below is honest about that: it tells the agent to go read the site first and then rebuild only the core loop locally.
coreLoopDIY: The agent reads the vendor's own site, picks the single workflow a paying customer repeats every week, and rebuilds just that workflow as a local Next.js app with SQLite persistence.
requirements: An agent with web access, since the feature set has to be read off the vendor's site before anything gets built
Patience for the moment the agent discovers the core loop depends on a third-party API
whatYouLose: Every integration, which in team tools is usually most of the actual value
Hosting, uptime and someone else's on-call rotation
Mobile and anything that has to reach a teammate who is not you
The long tail of features you did not notice on the pricing page but would have used by month three
Support, onboarding, and a vendor who cares when it breaks
moatNotes: Generic read, not a verified one: paid team tools of this size tend to defend themselves with connectors and polish rather than data.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the thing people buy is rarely the feature, it is the fact that the feature is already running, already connected to Slack or email or whatever else, and already working for the coworker who will not debug a local SQLite file. A personal rebuild is fine for a personal workflow and useless the moment a second human has to touch it. If the subscription is small and the workflow is daily, the honest answer is usually to keep paying and spend the weekend on something else.
notes: Listed on the strength of a pricing page and not much else; the verdict gets revisited once the product has been read end to end.
prompt:
Goal: build a local, single-user replacement for the core loop of the product at https://hellobutter.io, running entirely on my machine.

Step 0, research before any code:
1. Fetch https://hellobutter.io and https://hellobutter.io/pricing.
2. Write FINDINGS.md covering: what the product actually does, the one workflow a paying user repeats weekly, and which paid features are clearly pointless for a single user.
3. If the site is unreachable or the product is nothing like software, stop and tell me instead of guessing.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js App Router with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/app.db, schema in migrations/001_init.sql
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- Zod for all input validation

Build:
- One Next.js app using server actions, no separate API service.
- Implement only the single core workflow from FINDINGS.md, end to end, with real persistence.
- A seed script with realistic fake data so no screen is ever empty.
- A list view, a detail view, and create, edit, delete. No dashboard, no charts, no settings page.

Out of scope: auth, signup, multi-tenancy, billing, email sending, analytics, telemetry, Docker, deploy configs, and any test beyond one smoke test.

Rules:
- Any API key lives in .env.local, is read through process.env, and .env.local is gitignored. Never hardcode a secret.
- No third-party service calls unless FINDINGS.md proves the core loop is impossible without one. If so, isolate it behind a single adapter file and say so loudly in the README.
- Finish with README.md: how to run it, what you deliberately skipped, and an honest paragraph on the gap between this and the paid product.
